classification.genus: Alphapapillomavirus (and other genera, depending on type)

habitat.hostAssociation: Obligate human pathogen; over 100 genotypes identified, divided into low-risk and high-risk (oncogenic) types

identificationClues: HPV DNA testing (often combined with Pap cytology) is used for cervical cancer screening rather than viral culture, since HPV cannot be routinely cultured
Low-risk types (e.g. HPV-6, 11) cause genital warts; high-risk types (e.g. HPV-16, 18) are associated with cervical, anal, oropharyngeal, and other cancers
Most infections are transient and cleared by the immune system, but persistent high-risk infection is the key driver of HPV-associated cancer risk

diseases: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia and cervical cancer — high-risk types
Oropharyngeal, anal, vulvar, vaginal, and penile cancers — high-risk types
Common cutaneous warts — certain other HPV types
clinicalImportance.transmission: Direct skin-to-skin or mucosal contact, most often sexual contact for genital/oropharyngeal types
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: One of the most common sexually transmitted infections worldwide; the leading cause of cervical cancer globally; prophylactic vaccination (targeting the major high-risk and low-risk types) has substantially reduced HPV-related disease where uptake is high
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: HPV DNA co-testing alongside Pap cytology has become a standard part of cervical cancer screening in many guidelines, reflecting how central persistent high-risk HPV infection is to cervical carcinogenesis

examFacts.importantDisease: Genital warts; cervical and other anogenital/oropharyngeal cancers
examFacts.importantTest: HPV DNA testing, often paired with Pap cytology
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: Divided into low-risk (wart-causing) and high-risk (oncogenic) genotypes with distinct clinical significance
